newsitem.title: USA: AT&T CEO says stock boost top priority.
newsitem.headline: AT&T CEO says stock boost top priority.

text.p: AT&T Corp. Chairman Robert Allen told shareowners at the company's annual meeting on Wednesday that boosting AT&T's flagging stock price is management's highest priority.

"It's priced much too low," Allen said of AT&T's stock price in speech to shareholders. "That's disappointing to you, and it's totally unacceptable to us. The leadership of AT&T has no greater priority than to increase shareowner value."
A year ago, the stock closed at $45. The stock closed Wednesday at $34.625 up 37.50 cents. Three weeks ago, in late April, it hit $30.75, a 52-week low.
Historic comparisons are complicated due to the 1996 divestiture of Lucent Technologies Inc. and NCR Corp., AT&T's former equipment and computer arms.
AT&T stock remains the nation's most widely held publicly listed stock, with more than 3.3 million shareholders owning about 1.6 billion shares, according to a company spokesman.
Allen told reporters prior to his speech that AT&T was considering options to increase share value, including buybacks, but it had no plans to do so currently.
Later, in response to a shareholder's question, Allen said AT&T was continuing to look at its dividend policy.
He emphasized that the company' fundamentals remain very strong, but reiterated that shareholders will have to accept lower earnings in return for future growth.

"This is the classic long-term/short-term tradeoff. We're accepting lower short-term earnings in return for substantial long-term growth," he said. His plan was to deliver earnings per share of $5 to $6 a year in five years. That translates into annual operating earnings of $8 billion to $10 billion a year, compared with the $5.6 billion the company recorded in 1996.
Allen's comments appeared designed to stave off criticism of the performance of AT&T's stock, but some dissatisfied shareholders nonetheless took aim at his leadership.
"The guidance here looks like the Titanic and you are captain," shareholder Philip Rybakowski said of the turbulent changes at the company.
But other shareholders were satisfied with overall performance, noting the difficult transformation into a company focused on communications services, not manufacturing.
"I am a little bit disappointed," said Warren Wilhide of Morristown, N.J. "But in total, it's pretty good.

"They are laying a foundation for the future," he added, referring to AT&T's plans to spend $8 billion to $9 billion more in 1997 to compete in businesses such as local service, wireless, and information services.
Ninety-one percent of shareholders voted in favor of a proposal to broaden AT&T's long-term share incentive program to include middle-management and to improve the employee share option plan.

All five shareowner proposals were defeated. They included one that would have forced AT&T board members to disclose political contributions and another that would nullify stock options to managers who leave before retirement.
The 10 nominees for board of directors were elected, including two outside board members and John Walter, AT&T's president and chief operating officer.
